meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'bar, pub' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Our bar is closing.

examples.text: Проверьте все бары и старых друзей.
examples.trans: Check all the bars and old friends.
It is already morning. Our bar is closing.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'bartender', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: The bartender poured the wine.

examples.text: Бармен, принесите нам бокал белого вина!
examples.trans: Bartender, bring us a glass of white wine!

examples.text: Бармен наливает холодную воду в стакан.
examples.trans: The bartender pours cold water into the glass.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'bar' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.

examples.trans: He approached the bar counter.

examples.text: Вы можете подождать за барной стойкой.
examples.trans: You can wait at the bar counter.

examples.text: Что ты вообще делаешь за нашей барной стойкой?
examples.trans: What are you even doing behind our bar counter?

meanings.note: + genitive: 'бояться собак'. Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be afraid (of), to fear'.

examples.trans: We have nobody to fear here.
I'm not afraid.

examples.text: Это наш город. Нам здесь бояться некого.
examples.trans: This is our town. We have nobody to fear here.

meanings.note: + prepositional (where). Core Russian prep meaning 'in, into' in everyday speech.
+ accusative (where to). Core Russian prep meaning 'in, into' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Руки вверх = hands up. Core Russian adv meaning 'up, upwards' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Look: hands up, surrender!
To look up.

examples.text: Ваш рейтинг снова резко растёт вверх!
examples.trans: Your rating is sharply rising again!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'at all'.

examples.text: Я вовсе не хочу спорить с вами.
examples.trans: I do not want to argue with you at all.

examples.text: Вовсе нет, я жду хозяина ресторана.
examples.trans: Not at all, I am waiting for the restaurant owner.
These are not silly jokes at all.

meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people

meanings.en: other forms: вас (gen/acc), вам (dat), вами (instr), вас (prep)
meanings.note: Case forms. Core Russian pron meaning 'you (polite or plural)' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: As you all know...
Does the governor support you?

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: imperative держи! when handing something over
imperative держи! when handing something over
Держи его!. Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to hold'.

examples.trans: Here you go, this is for you.
Grab him!
All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'design', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Мне нравится дизайн этого красивого меню.
examples.trans: I like the design of this beautiful menu.
Really? I am studying the original design.

meanings.note: + accusative. Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to wait, to expect', paired with 'подождать'.
Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to wait, to expect', paired with 'подождать'.

examples.trans: Don't wait for me.
I'm waiting for you.

meanings.note: Спасибо за + accusative. Core Russian prep meaning 'for; behind' in everyday speech.
+ instrumental. Core Russian prep meaning 'for; behind' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Thank you for your trust!
Thanks for the present.
What for?

meanings.note: Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to block', forming an aspectual pair with 'загородить'.

examples.trans: Do not block the walkway for other people.
Please do not block the walkway for the waiters.

meanings.note: Зал суда = courtroom. Common masculine noun meaning 'hall, large room; courtroom' in everyday Russian.
Regional/colloquial. Common masculine noun meaning 'hall, large room; courtroom' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Please enter the courtroom.
A big hall.
Understood. And who is managing the dining room?

meanings.note: Location. Core Russian adv meaning 'here' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: I'm here.
We live here.
But we're in business here.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'idea' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Good idea!

examples.text: Хорошая идея! Я сейчас же попробую.
examples.trans: Good idea! I will try right now.
I have an excellent idea!

meanings.note: Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to study', forming an aspectual pair with 'изучить'.

examples.trans: The student carefully studies the new rule.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'column', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Он спрятался за высокой колонной в зале.
examples.trans: He hid behind a tall column in the hall.

examples.text: Хозяин точно не стоит за этой колонной.
examples.trans: The owner definitely is not standing behind this pillar.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'someone', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Кто-то не оценил твой отличный ход?
examples.trans: Did someone not appreciate your great move?
Finally someone is for the people!

examples.text: Слушай, тут пишут: «Гордость России! Наконец-то кто-то за народ!»
examples.trans: Listen, here they write: 'Pride of Russia! Finally someone is for the people!'

meanings.note: on a phone or in a restaurant; indeclinable

examples.trans: What's this menu here?
The menu, please.

examples.text: Что за меню здесь? Как позвонить?
examples.trans: What's this menu here? How do I make a call?

мешать.gloss: to be in the way, to disturb

meanings.en: to be in the way, to hinder
meanings.note: + dative. Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be in the way, to disturb', paired with 'помешать'.
Не мешай! = Don't bother me!. Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be in the way, to disturb', paired with 'помешать'.

examples.trans: The radiators are in the way.
Don't bother me!

examples.text: Филиппыч, миксер проехать не может. Радиаторы мешают.
examples.trans: Filippych, the mixer truck can't get through. The radiators are in the way.

meanings.note: молодой человек = young man (polite address)

examples.text: Молодой человек, как на тест-драйв записаться?
examples.trans: Young man, how do I sign up for a test drive?

examples.text: Молодой человек, а как на тест-драйв записаться?
examples.trans: Young man, how do I sign up for a test drive?

meanings.note: + infinitive. Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can, to be able', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.trans: Pour me some tea.

Nina, pour your husband a drink. We've got something to celebrate!

meanings.note: Derived masculine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'drink'.

examples.text: Ты совсем не пьёшь крепкие напитки?

examples.text: Не говори об этом никому, ладно?

meanings.note: Stronger contrast than 'а'. Core Russian conj meaning 'but' in everyday speech.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Russian uses one word for both. Common feminine noun meaning 'leg, foot' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Come in. Please put your right foot on the bed.

meanings.note: + prepositional; об before a vowel: об этом

examples.trans: I'm thinking about it.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'original' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.

examples.trans: The chef invented an original soup recipe.

meanings.en: to rest, relax, be on holiday

examples.text: Всё отлично, отдыхай! Сегодня выходные, всё круто!
examples.trans: Everything is great, get some rest! It is the weekend today, everything is cool!

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('excellent').

examples.trans: It'll be an excellent flat.
An excellent area!

examples.text: Квартира будет отличная. На Симашко есть новый дом.
examples.trans: It'll be an excellent flat. There's a new building on Simashko Street.

meanings.note: From German 'Offiziant' / Late Latin 'officians' (one who performs a duty or service).

examples.trans: The waiter politely greets the new guests.
Please do not block the walkway for the waiters.
To command the waiters.

meanings.note: Подожди! = wait!. Used as a perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to wait (a while)', paired with 'ждать'.

examples.trans: Wait, I'll be right there.
Wait a minute.

examples.text: Подожди, Нин, ты не поняла. Это же стыдно!

meanings.note: Handing something over.
Answer to thanks.
Handing something over.

examples.trans: A coffee, please.

meanings.note: On foot. Used as a perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to go (set off)', paired with 'идти'.

examples.trans: May I go?
Let's go home.
Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Informal. Core Russian interj meaning 'bye' in everyday speech.
As an adverb. Core Russian interj meaning 'bye' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Bye!

Bye, darling!

meanings.note: + dative. Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'мочь'). Used as a perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to help', paired with 'помогать'.

examples.trans: Maybe you could help?
Of course I'll help.

examples.text: Экскаваторщик — это не мой уровень. Может, поможешь?
examples.trans: Excavator driver isn't my level. Maybe you could help?

meanings.note: понимаешь? = you know? do you understand?

examples.trans: I understand.

examples.text: Я хочу нормально жить! Я хочу биде, понимаешь?
examples.trans: I want to live like a normal person! I want a bidet, do you understand?

meanings.note: as a side word: Правда, всё нормально = Honestly, everything's fine
as a side word: Правда, всё нормально = Honestly, everything's fine

examples.trans: Honestly, everything's fine.

examples.text: Правда, Нин, всё нормально. Скажи что-нибудь, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: Honestly, Nina, everything's fine. Say something, please.

meanings.note: 'это просто' = it's easy. Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I'm just tired.
It's easy.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'passage', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Широкий проход ведёт прямо на кухню.
examples.trans: A wide passage leads straight to the kitchen.
Please do not block the walkway for the waiters.

meanings.note: Dining establishment. Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.trans: They called from the Italian restaurant.
In the evening they went to a restaurant.

examples.text: Кстати, звонили из итальянского ресторана. Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: By the way, they called from the Italian restaurant. They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'thank you' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Thanks, Dad!
Thank you for your trust!

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'counter'.

examples.text: Костя протёр барную стойку чистым полотенцем.

examples.text: Вы можете подождать за барной стойкой.

examples.trans: You spilled milk all over the counter!

meanings.note: the infinitive 'Стоять!' as a police order
the infinitive 'Стоять!' as a police order

examples.trans: Freeze!

examples.text: То есть просто стоять и смотреть?
examples.trans: So we just stand and watch?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Я точно не помню его адрес.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'owner', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Вовсе нет, я жду хозяина ресторана.
examples.trans: Not at all, I am waiting for the restaurant owner.

meanings.note: + infinitive or a noun. Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: He is a good person.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to read', paired with 'прочитать'.

examples.trans: You don't read the small print.

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.
